triage.name: Hydronephrosis
triage.reason: Radiographic finding rather than a single diagnosis; better taught through its underlying causes (obstruction, stones, tumors) than as a standalone case.

demographics: Slightly more common in males, reflecting the higher prevalence of obstructive uropathy such as benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostate cancer
More common in older adults because of prostatic disease and pelvic malignancy

chief_complaints.text: I'm passing much less urine than usual
I feel like I need to throw up

hpi.onset: Depends on the cause: sudden and severe with an obstructing stone, gradual and vague with a slow-growing tumor or chronic bladder outlet obstruction
hpi.duration: Hours to days when acute; weeks to months when chronic
hpi.progression: Acute obstruction causes steadily worsening pain; chronic obstruction may cause little pain and is instead noticed through declining kidney function or an incidental imaging finding
hpi.location: One or both flanks, sometimes radiating toward the groin or lower abdomen
hpi.radiation: From the flank toward the groin, labia or testicle when a stone is the cause
hpi.quality: Dull and constant with gradual obstruction; sharp and colicky with an obstructing stone
hpi.severity: Mild and vague when chronic; severe when acute obstruction causes renal capsule stretching
hpi.timing: Constant when due to obstruction; may come in waves when a stone is moving
relieving: Nothing reliably; opioids or passage of the stone may help

associated_symptoms.text: Passing much less urine than usual
Swelling of the legs and ankles

pertinent_negatives: Pain that is clearly colicky and radiates to the groin in a patient with no stone history
Recent sick contacts with the same illness

positives.text: Passing much less urine than usual

argues_against: Sudden one-sided pelvic pain with vomiting

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may present with irritability, poor feeding, vomiting or a palpable abdominal mass rather than flank pain.
Chronic obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia or malignancy often causes no pain; patients present with fatigue, confusion, edema or an incidental imaging finding.
Physiologic dilation of the collecting system is common in pregnancy, so hydronephrosis may be an incidental finding; when symptomatic it usually causes right-sided flank pain.
Patients with chronic kidney disease may have little pain and present instead with worsening renal function or fluid overload.

general.moderate: Uncomfortable, shifts position, mild distress with movement
general.severe: Ill-appearing, diaphoretic, splints the affected side, reluctant to move
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, lethargic, may be confused if uremic or septic

labs.caveat: Rises with obstruction; a normal creatinine does not exclude unilateral or early obstruction.
Often rises disproportionately to creatinine in obstructive uropathy.
Hyperkalemia from reduced distal potassium excretion; can be life-threatening and drives urgent decompression.
Metabolic acidosis from impaired acid excretion.
Hyponatremia can occur with volume overload or diuretic use.
Leukocytosis suggests infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) or concurrent urinary tract infection.
Elevated lactate with fever and obstruction suggests sepsis from pyonephrosis and warrants urgent decompression.
Hematuria is common with stones, tumors or infection causing the obstruction.
Pyuria suggests infection or inflammation; sterile pyuria can occur with obstruction alone.
Positive nitrite supports a gram-negative urinary tract infection complicating the obstruction.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging and to exclude pregnancy-related causes of hydronephrosis.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line in most patients, especially children, pregnancy and renal impairment (no radiation, no contrast)

findings.text: Dilated renal pelvis and calyces (anechoic fluid-filled spaces)
Blunted or effaced renal papillae with a rounded, ballooned collecting system
Thinning of the renal cortex when obstruction is chronic
Dilated ureter proximal to the obstruction
Residual urine in the bladder after voiding (bladder outlet obstruction)
Grading by severity: mild (pelvis only), moderate (pelvis and calyces), severe (marked calyceal dilation with cortical thinning)

imaging.preferred_when: When a stone, tumor or the exact level of obstruction needs to be defined

Mass lesion causing extrinsic or intrinsic obstruction (tumor, lymph node, retroperitoneal fibrosis)
Delayed excretion of contrast on the affected side with a nephrogram
Perinephric stranding or fluid suggesting forniceal rupture or infection

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected obstructing stone when contrast is not needed or renal function is impaired

findings.text: Perinephric stranding and ureteral wall thickening at the stone

imaging.study: Magnetic resonance urography (MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast)
imaging.preferred_when: Pregnancy or when CT contrast is contraindicated and ultrasound is nondiagnostic

findings.text: Dilated renal pelvis, calyces and ureter with the level of obstruction
Extrinsic mass or fibrosis compressing the ureter

imaging.preferred_when: Rarely used now; largely replaced by CT urography

findings.text: Delayed opacification and dilation of the collecting system on the affected side
Usually nonspecific; may show a radio-opaque calculus or renal outline enlargement

imaging.preferred_when: Children with suspected vesicoureteral reflux or posterior urethral valves

Assesses creatinine, potassium, bicarbonate and sodium to gauge renal function and urgency
Looks for hematuria, pyuria, nitrite and bacteria suggesting stone or infection
Excludes pregnancy and guides imaging choice
initial.only_if: patient is a woman of childbearing age

confirmatory.why: Defines the level and cause of obstruction (stone, tumor, stricture) and guides intervention

confirmatory.why: Defines an obstructing stone when contrast is unnecessary or renal function is impaired
confirmatory.only_if: suspected nephrolithiasis or contrast is contraindicated

Suggests sepsis from pyonephrosis and need for urgent decompression
supporting.only_if: fever, hypotension or clinical suspicion of sepsis

supporting.test: Magnetic resonance urography (MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast)
supporting.only_if: pregnant or contrast contraindicated and ultrasound nondiagnostic

supporting.why: Evaluates reflux or posterior urethral valves
supporting.only_if: child with recurrent urinary tract infection or suspected reflux

not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management when ultrasound or CT is available
Obsolete; CT urography is more informative
Not needed unless the pain is epigastric or pancreatitis is suspected

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Ultrasound first in children, pregnancy and renal impairment; CT when the cause or level of obstruction must be defined
Fever with obstruction (pyonephrosis) or hyperkalemia/acidosis requires urgent decompression, not just antibiotics
Bilateral hydronephrosis or a solitary obstructed kidney is a urologic emergency
Bladder outlet obstruction with a distended bladder is relieved by catheterization

differential.name: Nephrolithiasis
differential.why_considered: An obstructing stone is the most common cause of acute hydronephrosis and presents with severe flank pain, nausea and hematuria.
differential.trigger: Sudden, severe, colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with hematuria

history: Abrupt onset of severe colicky pain
Pain radiates from the flank to the groin, labia or testicle
Restless, cannot find a comfortable position
exam: Costovertebral angle tenderness on the affected side
labs: Creatinine may be normal or mildly elevated
imaging: Radio-opaque calculus with proximal hydroureteronephrosis on non-contrast CT
Ureteral wall thickening and perinephric stranding at the stone

differential.name: Pyelonephritis
differential.why_considered: Infection of the kidney can cause flank pain, fever and leukocytosis, and may coexist with or mimic obstructive hydronephrosis.
differential.trigger: Fever, chills and flank pain with pyuria or positive nitrite

history: Dysuria, frequency or urgency preceding the flank pain
imaging: Ultrasound may be normal or show mild dilation without a clear transition point
CT may show focal wedge-shaped hypodensity or perinephric stranding without an obstructing lesion

differential.name: Renal cell carcinoma
differential.why_considered: A renal mass can obstruct the collecting system or present as an incidental finding with hematuria and flank pain.
differential.trigger: Hematuria, flank mass or unexplained weight loss with a solid renal lesion on imaging

history: Weight loss, night sweats or malaise
imaging: Solid enhancing renal mass on contrast CT or MRI
Dilation of the collecting system distal to the mass

differential.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
differential.why_considered: Bladder outlet obstruction from an enlarged prostate is a common cause of bilateral hydronephrosis, especially in older men.

history: Gradual onset of urinary hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia and incomplete emptying
exam: Enlarged, firm, smooth prostate on digital rectal exam
imaging: Bilateral hydronephrosis with a thick-walled bladder and post-void residual urine

differential.name: Ovarian torsion
differential.why_considered: Sudden one-sided lower abdominal or flank pain with nausea and vomiting can mimic an obstructing stone.
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of severe one-sided pelvic pain with vomiting at the start

labs: Negative or positive hCG depending on pregnancy status
imaging: Enlarged ovary with reduced or absent Doppler flow on ultrasound

differential.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal or flank pain in a person who could be pregnant can present with pain and adnexal findings.
differential.trigger: Any patient of childbearing age with abdominal pain

imaging: No intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound

differential.name: Diabetes insipidus
differential.why_considered: Polyuria and polydipsia can lead to dilated collecting systems from high urine flow, and can be confused with obstructive hydronephrosis.

imaging: Mild bilateral dilation without a transition point

differential.name: Simple renal cyst
differential.why_considered: A large cyst can compress the collecting system and cause hydronephrosis-like dilation on imaging.

imaging: Well-circumscribed anechoic lesion with imperceptible wall on ultrasound
No communication with the collecting system

severity.mild: Mild dilation of the renal pelvis only, normal creatinine, no or minimal pain, no fever, no obstruction on imaging
severity.moderate: Dilation of the pelvis and calyces, mild to moderate flank pain, creatinine 1.4–2.5 mg/dL, may have nausea and vomiting
severity.severe: Marked calyceal dilation with cortical thinning, severe pain, creatinine 2.0–5.0 mg/dL, possible hyperkalemia or acidosis, may have fever if infected
severity.critical: Bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a solitary kidney with anuria, creatinine >4.0 mg/dL, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, sepsis from pyonephrosis, or uremic encephalopathy

red_flags.meaning: Suggests pyonephrosis or infected obstructed system; requires urgent decompression, not just antibiotics
Bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a solitary kidney; a urologic emergency
Life-threatening electrolyte disturbance from renal failure; needs immediate treatment and decompression
Possible sepsis from pyonephrosis; needs resuscitation and urgent decompression
Worsening obstruction or acute kidney injury; requires urgent urologic evaluation

red_flags.finding: Palpable flank mass with weight loss
red_flags.meaning: Suggests underlying malignancy; needs prompt imaging and referral

complications.name: Hypertension
clues: Elevated blood pressure after relief of obstruction

special_populations.differences: Often presents with irritability, poor feeding, vomiting or a palpable abdominal mass rather than flank pain; common causes include vesicoureteral reflux and posterior urethral valves; ultrasound is first-line and VCUG may be needed.

Chronic obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia or malignancy often causes no pain; patients present with fatigue, confusion, edema or an incidental imaging finding; higher risk of renal failure and hyperkalemia.

Physiologic dilation of the collecting system is common, especially on the right; when symptomatic it causes right-sided flank pain; ultrasound and MRI without contrast are preferred to avoid radiation.
Patients with chronic kidney disease may have little pain and present with worsening renal function or fluid overload; contrast studies should be avoided when possible.
Diabetic patients are at higher risk of urinary tract infections and papillary necrosis, which can complicate or mimic obstruction.

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the pain, and does it radiate anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Flank or back pain, sometimes radiating toward the groin, labia or testicle when a stone is the cause

key_questions.question: How did the pain start, and how has it changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden severe colicky pain suggests an obstructing stone; gradual, vague or absent pain suggests chronic obstruction from tumor or bladder outlet obstruction

key_questions.question: How much urine are you passing compared with normal?
key_questions.looking_for: Oliguria or anuria suggests bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a solitary kidney, a urologic emergency

key_questions.question: Have you noticed blood in your urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Hematuria, which points to a stone, tumor or infection as the cause

key_questions.question: Do you have fever, chills or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever with obstruction suggests pyonephrosis or an infected obstructed system and requires urgent decompression

key_questions.question: Have you had kidney stones before, and have you ever passed one?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior stone episodes, which make an obstructing stone the likely cause

key_questions.question: Have you had any trouble starting your stream, a weak stream, dribbling or getting up at night to urinate?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual lower urinary tract symptoms suggesting benign prostatic hyperplasia or bladder outlet obstruction

key_questions.question: Have you had any pelvic or abdominal surgery, or radiation to the pelvis?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior pelvic surgery or radiation, which can cause ureteral stricture or obstruction

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have cancer, or have you had unexplained weight loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Pelvic or retroperitoneal malignancy causing extrinsic obstruction

key_questions.question: Do you have any condition that affects your bladder control, such as a spinal cord injury or multiple sclerosis?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurogenic bladder as a cause of incomplete emptying and upper tract dilation

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including anything for bladder or urinary symptoms?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticholinergics such as oxybutynin, tolterodine, amitriptyline or diphenhydramine, which can worsen urinary retention

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy, which changes the imaging approach and can itself cause physiologic hydronephrosis

key_questions.question: Have you had burning with urination, urgency or frequency?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms of urinary tract infection, which can complicate or mimic obstruction

key_questions.question: Have you noticed swelling in your legs or ankles, or feeling more tired than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Edema or fatigue suggesting chronic kidney disease or fluid overload from renal failure

reasoning_points: Flank or back pain with costovertebral angle tenderness on the affected side
Nausea, vomiting and hematuria suggesting an obstructing stone
Oliguria or anuria pointing to bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a solitary kidney
Fever with obstruction raising concern for pyonephrosis and the need for urgent decompression
Elevated creatinine and BUN with hyperkalemia or metabolic acidosis indicating obstructive nephropathy
Risk factors such as nephrolithiasis, benign prostatic hyperplasia, pelvic malignancy or neurogenic bladder
Imaging showing a dilated renal pelvis and calyces, with the level and cause of obstruction identified
Pregnancy excluded before CT imaging in anyone who could be pregnant

easy: Classic colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with hematuria
Costovertebral angle tenderness on the affected side
Ultrasound showing a dilated collecting system with an obstructing stone
medium: Older man with gradual lower urinary tract symptoms and bilateral hydronephrosis from benign prostatic hyperplasia
Chronic obstruction with little pain, presenting with fatigue, edema or an incidental imaging finding
Mild pyuria or hematuria on urinalysis without a clear stone history
Pregnant patient with right-sided flank pain and physiologic dilation of the collecting system
hard: Afebrile older adult with a normal white count and slowly rising creatinine from chronic obstruction
Patient with pelvic malignancy causing extrinsic ureteral obstruction and no urinary symptoms
Child with irritability, poor feeding and a palpable abdominal mass rather than flank pain
Fever with obstruction (pyonephrosis) presenting as sepsis without classic flank pain
Anuria from obstruction of a solitary kidney or bilateral obstruction
